newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Marine-based Keppel sinks to 3-year low.
newsitem.headline: Marine-based Keppel sinks to 3-year low.

text.p: Shares in Singapore's maritime conglomerate Keppel Corporation Ltd shares sank to a three-year low on Friday, hammered by a bleak outlook for global shiprepair and poor national economic data.
The company, often seen as a core holding for fund managers looking to buy in Singapore, has interests ranging from ship repair and property development to banking and telecommunications.
Analysts said investors were disenchanted with Keppel and the company's shares had lost about 10 percent of their value after it posted a fall in 1996 earnings 10 days ago.
The shares hit Singapore $9.10, down 35 cents from Thursday, in moderately active trading on Friday afternoon with more than a million shares changing hands.
Poor sentiment was further compounded by the release of poor export data on Thursday as Singapore reported a 7.9 percent decline in non-oil exports for February, the fourth consecutive monthly drop.

"Keppel is seen as Singapore Inc. If investors are negative on Singapore, they are going to be negative on the stock as well," David Leow, an associate director with James Capel Research, told Reuters.
Keppel, which owns Singapore's largest ship repair yard, is expected to see flat earnings for the current year.
"Its earnings growth is going to be very weak this year. There is no organic growth," said an analyst with a local brokerage house.
Analysts said the only bright spots in the group's business were banking, through Keppel Bank, and in property from Keppel Land.

The long awaited recovery in ship repair business was unlikely to materialise in the near term as the problem is a structural one with Singapore facing over-capacity and high wage costs, analysts said.
Keppel added 360,000 dead weight tonne in capacity for ship repair last year but ship repair turnover actually fell about about 20 percent.
"The region faces a 44-percent over-capacity in large dry docks. It is difficult to see demand picking up in the near term. Neither do I see too sharp an improvement," Leow said.
Without a regular customer pool, Keppel suffers more than the other local yard like SembCorp or Jurong Shipyard, analysts said.
But some analysts said that in the longer term, they still liked the group's increasing exposure to telecommunications.
Through Keppel Telecommunications & Transportation, the group has a 35 percent stake in Singapores' second cellular phone operator MobileOne.

"MobileOne, Singapore's second cellular phone service provider, will provide a steadily growing recurrent earnings base by 1999," said Janice Chua, an analyst at Vickers Ballas Investment Research in her latest report.
Analysts also expect MobileOne to bid for a license to operate basic telephone services from 2000.
"If you trade on fundamentals, now is a good time to pick up on the stock," Leow said, sharing other analyst views that the group's future growth would not come from its ship repair operations.
